narrative.text: Cover page for The MAPS Toolkit: mHealth Assessment and Planning for Scale, published with the Global mHealth Initiative at Johns Hopkins University, WHO, HRP, and the United Nations Foundation.

Provides WHO Library Cataloguing-in-Publication data (ISBN 978 92 4 150951 0, NLM classification WA 310), 2015 copyright and licensing notices, legal disclaimers, cover photo credit (D-tree International eNutrition application in Zanzibar), and suggested citation for The MAPS Toolkit.

Presents the table of contents for The MAPS Toolkit, covering the front matter, introduction, project overview sheet, the six axes of scale (Groundwork, Partnerships, Financial health, Technology & architecture, Operations, and Monitoring & evaluation—each with a thematic overview, self-assessment questions, and planning and guidance), the summary scorecard, references, and two annexes.

Foreword by Flavia Bustreo (WHO) and Kate Dodson (United Nations Foundation) tracing the origins of the MAPS Toolkit to the Every Woman Every Child (EWEC) Innovation Working Group (IWG) Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism established by Norway in 2011 across 15 countries, and positioning the Toolkit for the transition from the Millennium Development Goals to the Sustainable Development Goals.

Acknowledges the authors (Jessica Rothstein and Tigest Tamrat under the guidance of Garrett Mehl at WHO and Alain Labrique at JHU-GmI), technical contributors, field experts, country-level partner organizations, testing and validation reviewers, the 26 IWG Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism projects, and Norad/WHO leadership.

Executive summary introducing the MAPS Toolkit as an iterative self-assessment and planning guide for project managers and teams already deploying an mHealth product, structured around six axes of scale: Groundwork, Partnerships, Financial health, Technology & architecture, Operations, and Monitoring & evaluation.

Lists acronyms and abbreviations used throughout the MAPS Toolkit, spanning digital health standards and systems (API, DHIS, eLMIS, HL7, HMIS, HRIS, ICD, OCL, OpenHIE, OpenSRP, SNOMED CT), organizations and networks (AeHIN, ANDH, CHAI, GSMA, HRP, ITU, IWG, JHU-GmI, KEMRI, MAMA, Norad, PMNCH, UNF, WHO), and mHealth programmes (m4RH, mNDCC, MOTECH, TextIT).

First half of the Key terminology glossary (Architecture through Mobile money), defining core mHealth and scale-up concepts including champions, client beneficiaries, core partners, data dashboard, data dictionary, data privacy, data quality assurance, data standards, eHealth, enabling environment, end-users, endgame, evaluation and formative research, health system constraints, interoperability, latency, mHealth strategy, and mobile aggregator.

Second half of the Key terminology glossary (Mobile network operator through Value proposition), defining MNOs, payers (distinguished from funders), pilot testing, process monitoring, mHealth product, programme fidelity, scaling up, secondary users, SMS, software, standard operating procedures (SOPs), stress tests, sustainability, total cost of ownership (TCO), value chain analysis, and value proposition.
Section divider page introducing the Introduction chapter of the MAPS Toolkit.

Provides background on scaling up mHealth in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), contrasting small-scale pilots and broad ecosystem-level literature with the MAPS Toolkit's actionable, project-level approach to continuous scale-up and sustainability, alongside sidebar definitions of scaling up, sustainability, and the three endgame models (government adoption, commercial adoption, and hybrid).

Explains the dual purpose of the MAPS Toolkit—Assess (via scored self-assessment questions) and Plan (via targeted guidance)—and introduces the cyclical Assess–Plan–Improve conceptual model (Figure 1) and the six axes of scale (Figure 2) with concise one-sentence descriptions of each axis.

Presents Figure 3 mapping the six axes of scale to their constituent domains (Parameters of scale, Contextual environment, Scientific basis; Strategic engagement, Partnership sustainability; Financial management, Financial model; Data, Interoperability, Adaptability; Personnel, Training & support, Outreach & sensitization, Contingency planning; Process monitoring, Evaluation research) and summarizes how MAPS was developed under the Norad-funded UNF–WHO IWG Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism.

Describes the three-part chapter structure for each axis (A. Thematic overview, B. Self-assessment, and C. Planning and guidance with Tips and considerations, Lessons from the field, and Resources) and specifies the target audience and eligibility criteria for projects using MAPS (deployed mHealth product past proof-of-concept with a defined mHealth strategy and scale-up endgame).

Explains how to conduct the MAPS self-assessment (either via individual specialist completion followed by a team review or via sequential team meetings over 1.5–2 hours), when to use the Toolkit as a baseline and periodic tracking tool, and how to respond to self-assessment questions using No/Yes or the four-stage progression (No, In progress, Performed, Documented) plus Not applicable (N/A).

Provides Table 1 defining and illustrating the four response options (No = 0, In progress = 1, Performed = 2, Documented = 3) using electricity constraints from SAQ 14-1 (solar chargers for health workers), and explains the three-level scoring system (overall, axis, and domain scores) using axis scorecards and the final scorecard.

Explains how project teams should use SAQ results to identify weak domains, consult planning resources, and periodically course-correct, accompanied by Figure 4 illustrating a worked sample SAQ (14-1 on addressing connectivity and electricity constraints, earning 4 out of 9 points).

Presents the baseline Project overview sheet worksheet capturing Project Details (date, project and organization names, mHealth strategy, technologies and communication channels), Current Project Status (coverage, start date and duration, operating geographies), and Vision for Scale (scale-up goals and anticipated time frame).
Chapter divider page for Axis 1: Groundwork, highlighting its position among the six axes of scale.

Introduces the Axis 1 (Groundwork) thematic overview across its three domains (Domain 1: Parameters of scale, Domain 2: Contextual environment, Domain 3: Scientific basis) and details Domain 1, guiding teams to articulate target health outcomes, health system constraints, scale-up metrics, quantifiable targets, and eligible population denominators.

Presents Table 2 on metrics for measuring scale-up success—Growth (client, e.g. FHI 360 m4RH in Tanzania), Adoption (institutional, e.g. KEMRI TextIT in Kenya), and Expansion (geo-political, e.g. JSI cStock across all 29 districts in Malawi)—Defines government adoption, commercial adoption (e.g. Changamka Linda Jamii with Safaricom), and hybrid endgames, and introduces Domain 2 (Contextual environment) covering policy and technical environments.

Completes Domain 2 with mHealth landscape assessment and details Domain 3 (Scientific basis), explaining how to align with validated health interventions, evaluate the four stages of mHealth evidence (Functionality, Usability, Efficacy, and Effectiveness), validate strategy components, and conduct local formative research and cultural contextualization.

Presents the Axis 1 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 1 (Parameters of scale, 8 points total), specifically SAQ 1-1 (6 points) on articulating RMNCH life-stage health outcomes and interventions, targeted health system constraints (availability, cost, efficiency, quality, utilization, information, acceptability), and operationalized scale-up metrics (growth, adoption, geo-political expansion).

Continues Axis 1 self-assessment with SAQ 1-2 (2 points) on specifying the endgame strategy (government adoption, commercial adoption, or hybrid) and Domain 2 (Contextual environment, 22 points total), covering SAQ 2-1 (6 points) on national health/eHealth policy alignment and working group participation and SAQ 2-2 (8 points) on network coverage and electricity reach and reliability.

Presents SAQ 2-3 (8 points) on assessing the local mHealth landscape and Domain 3 (Scientific basis, 30 points total), including SAQ 3-1a (8 points) on evidence across functionality, usability, efficacy, and effectiveness and SAQ 3-1b (4 points) on validating content and operational procedures against evidence-based guidelines or pilot studies.

Presents SAQ 3-2 (18 points, scored 0–3 across No, In progress, Performed, and Documented) assessing local appropriateness across six items: formative research, pilot study in a comparable setting, local health system constraints, local health service capacity, integration with health worker workflows, and sociocultural/gender norms.

Provides the Axis 1 (Groundwork) scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 1: Parameters of scale (8 points), Domain 2: Contextual environment (22 points), and Domain 3: Scientific basis (30 points), and averaging the three domain percentages to obtain the overall Axis 1 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 1 and provides Domain 1 tips and frameworks for articulating how mHealth strategies address health system constraints and advance universal health coverage, citing Labrique et al. (2013) on 12 common applications and Mehl & Labrique (2014) on prioritizing integrated mHealth strategies.

Provides Domain 2 (Contextual environment) planning guidance on joining communities of practice and technical working groups to share knowledge and map the digital health environment, profiling the mHealth Working Group, Asia eHealth Information Network (AeHIN), African Network for Digital Health (ANDH), HealthEnabled Africa, and the ICT4CHW Google Group.

Provides Domain 3 (Scientific basis) guidance on leveraging the existing evidence base for health interventions, shares a field lesson from KEMRI's TextIT PMTCT SMS programme in Kenya on using focus group formative research to personalize messages and include male partners, and introduces JSI's Pathway to Supply Chain Sustainability planning tool for government adoption.

Summarizes four foundational planning and contextual-assessment resources for Axis 1: K4Health's mHealth Planning Guide (2014), HealthEnabled's How to Approach mHealth (Keisling, 2015), the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit (2012), and PMNCH's ICT for Women's and Children's Health: A Planning Workbook (2014).

Describes country-level feasibility and landscape-mapping resources for Axis 1: GSMA Country Feasibility Reports (2014) across 10 African countries, HealthEnabled African Digital Dashboards (2015), USAID/African Strategies for Health's mHealth Database, the Center for Health Market Innovations (CHMI) Health Program Database, and the mHealth Working Group Inventory.

Concludes the Axis 1 resource list with four global mHealth project repositories and compendia: the GSMA mHealth Tracker, the WHO–ITU Global eHealth Projects Repository, mRegistry.org (WHO HRP, JHU-GmI, UNICEF, mPowering Frontline Health Workers), and the USAID/ASH mHealth Compendium series.
Chapter divider page for Axis 2: Partnerships.

Introduces the Axis 2 (Partnerships) thematic overview across Domain 4 (Strategic engagement) and Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability), detailing how project teams assess internal competencies to identify core and supporting external partners and tailor value propositions to foster stakeholder buy-in.

Presents Table 3 mapping notions of value across seven potential partner types (MOH/government, MNO, field-level NGO/CBO, end-users, donors, academia, and insurers) and outlines Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability), emphasizing cultivating organizational champions and establishing formal governance structures (steering committees, MoUs, and vendor contracts).

Presents the Axis 2 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 4 (Strategic engagement, 48 points total), covering SAQ 4-1a (9 points) on defining internal competencies, required external partner types, and timing, and SAQ 4-1b (27 points) on partnership maturity across nine partner/vendor categories (MOH, financing, MNO/aggregator, NGO/CBO, technology, hardware/service, marketing, evaluation/research, and health content).

Continues Axis 2 self-assessment with SAQ 4-2 (12 points) on communicating the product's value proposition and alignment with partner, local government, and global health priorities, and introduces Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability, 50 points total) with SAQ 5-1a (9 points) on fostering champions and SAQ 5-1b (10 points) on evaluating the first champion's authority, stability, resources, scope awareness, and demonstrated commitment.

Concludes the Axis 2 Self-Assessment Questions with SAQ 5-1c (10 points) assessing a second champion's advocacy capacity, SAQ 5-2a (12 points) on inclusive governance mechanisms (representative steering committee, regular meetings, terms of reference, and partner feedback), and SAQ 5-2b (9 points) on shared agreement with core partners regarding project vision, scale-up scope/goals, and joint workplan/timeline.

Provides the Axis 2 (Partnerships) scorecard for calculating scores across Domain 4: Strategic engagement (48 points, with denominator adjustments for N/A items in SAQ 4-1b) and Domain 5: Partnership sustainability (50 points, or 30 points if champion questions 5-1b/5-1c are N/A), averaging the two domain percentages for the Axis 2 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 2 and Domain 4 (Strategic engagement), advising teams to map partners by both technical competencies and strategic assets (visibility, networks, gatekeepers) and sharing a field lesson on continuous engagement from MAMA South Africa's transition into the national Department of Health's MomConnect initiative.

Provides Domain 4 guidance on starting partner negotiations early to accommodate turnover and legal/MoU delays, articulating partner 'gives and gets' value propositions (illustrated by India's SERP mNDCC nutrition monitoring tool adopted by the Andhra Pradesh government and expanded to 6000 villages with the World Bank), and evaluating inter-departmental political dynamics and mandates.

Provides Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability) guidance on diversifying partners to avoid single-vendor lock-in, cultivating backup or team champions to mitigate political turnover, and positioning government at the forefront of coordination—illustrated by CHAI Malawi's MOH-convened RapidSMS steering committee and Rwanda's MOH eHealth Technical Working Group (TWG).

Advises teams to document partnership terms of engagement (roles, intellectual property/licensing, human and financial resource commitments, branding, and vendor billing structures) in MoUs and contracts, and summarizes two partnership resources: PMNCH's ICT for Women's and Children's Health Planning Workbook (2014) and the WHO & UNF Practical Guide for Engaging with Mobile Network Operators in mHealth for RMNCH (2015).

Concludes the Axis 2 resource list with four publications on MNO partnerships and governance: GSMA mWomen's Mutual Value, Mutual Gain (2014), Advanced Development for Africa's Scaling Up Mobile Health: Developing mHealth Partnerships for Scale (2013), Miller's Fifty Tips for Your Statement of Work (2007), and UNF's ICT4SOML Nigeria Situation Analysis (2013).
Chapter divider page for Axis 3: Financial health.

Introduces the Axis 3 (Financial health) thematic overview across Domain 6 (Financial management) and Domain 7 (Financial model), detailing programme costs (recurring fixed, variable, and one-time capital costs, in-kind contributions, cost-sharing, and regular budget revision) and end-user technology and non-technology costs.

Completes Domain 6 with health system costs (provider workload and supply ripple effects from increased care demand) and 5-year cost forecasting using total cost of ownership (TCO) and cost drivers, and details Domain 7 (Financial model), covering stakeholder value chain analysis, dynamic business planning, and diversifying funders and payers.

Presents the Axis 3 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 6 (Financial management, 45 points total), covering SAQ 6-1 (18 points) on programme-level expenditure tracking, phase-based costing, capital/recurring/variable categorization, in-kind valuation, cost-sharing, and budget revision protocols; SAQ 6-2 (6 points) on end-user technology and non-technology costs; and SAQ 6-3 (9 points) on health system demand, provider time, and commodity costs.

Continues Axis 3 self-assessment with SAQ 6-4 (12 points) on forecasting 5-year total cost of ownership, cost drivers, economies of scale, and costing assumptions/risks, and introduces Domain 7 (Financial model, 36 points total) with SAQ 7-1 (12 points) on value chain analysis and quantifying tangible/intangible status quo costs and SAQ 7-2 (12 points) on developing a shareable business, resource mobilization, and marketing plan.

Concludes the Axis 3 Self-Assessment Questions with SAQ 7-3 (12 points) on sustainable funding choices: exploring diverse funding streams (including non-health sectors), identifying main and alternative payers across the value chain, planning payer engagement, and mitigating payer-transition risks.

Provides the Axis 3 (Financial health) scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 6: Financial management (45 points) and Domain 7: Financial model (36 points), averaging the two percentages to compute the overall Axis 3 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 3 and Domain 6 (Financial management), highlighting commonly overlooked scale-up costs when forecasting: transition and capacity-building costs when transferring ownership to a Ministry of Health, technology adaptation and API integration costs, and legal/travel costs for advocacy and partner contract negotiation.

Outlines opportunities for minimizing mHealth programme expenditures in Axis 3 (Financial Health) across two major cost drivers—technology (conducting landscape analyses of existing platforms and weighing fixed versus variable costs of open-source versus proprietary software) and training programmes (exploring cost-effective delivery mechanisms such as blended mobile/electronic and face-to-face learning)—and illustrates a MOTECH Ghana costing exercise comparing voice versus SMS.

Provides Domain 7 (Financial Model) planning guidance on exploring routes to financial sustainability, featuring field lessons from VillageReach's comparison of four financial models for scaling up the Chipatala cha pa Foni hotline in Malawi (selecting a partnership and Airtel zero-rating cost-sharing model with GSMA support) and FHI 360's willingness-to-pay and partner solicitation assessments for transitioning m4RH from grant financing in Kenya and the United Republic of Tanzania, plus an overview of the Vital Wave Consulting/mHealth Alliance resource Sustainable Financing for mHealth (2010).

Lists five financial management and business model resources for Axis 3: Dimagi CommCare's Total Cost of Ownership Model (2014), Dalberg's Preparing the Next Generation of Community Health Workers: The Power of Technology (2012), Strategyzer's Business Model Canvas (2008), Osterwalder & Pigneur's The Business Model Generation (2009), and Strategyzer's The Value Proposition Design (2014).
Section divider page introducing Axis 4: Technology & Architecture within the six-axis MAPS Toolkit navigation framework.

Presents Section A (Thematic overview) for Axis 4: Technology & Architecture, defining the axis across Domain 8 (Data: 8-1 data access and quality, 8-2 data transmission and storage, 8-3 data security), Domain 9 (Interoperability: 9-1 systems integration, 9-2 data standards), and Domain 10 (Adaptability: 10-1 adaptability of technology, 10-2 adaptability of content, 10-3 transferability), detailing Domain 8 requirements for dashboards, automated data quality assurance, server latency, bandwidth, storage capacity, and stress testing, and defining key terms.

Concludes the Domain 8 overview on hardware/software data security and national patient privacy policies, and introduces Domain 9 (Interoperability), explaining how semantic and technology standards enable integration with national health management information systems (HMIS), outlining the three stages of achieving interoperability, defining interoperability and data standards, and presenting Table 4 on common health data standards (HL7, ICD-10, SNOMED CT, INN, and ISO).

Presents the thematic overview for Domain 10 (Adaptability) under Axis 4, covering adaptability of technology across user groups and health domains with documentation for local developers, adaptability of content for new sociocultural contexts, languages, and illiterate users (via multimedia or IVR), and transferability across diverse mobile devices and operating systems.

Presents Section B (Self-assessment questions) for Axis 4, Domain 8: Data, covering SAQ 8-1 on application features for data accessibility and quality (validation rules, real-time dashboards, data extraction/export, 9 points), SAQ 8-2 on data centre capacity for processing, latency, bandwidth, storage configuration, government hosting compliance, and stress testing (18 points), and SAQ 8-3a on server, access, device security, and breach response protocols (12 points).

Continues Axis 4 self-assessment questions with SAQ 8-3b on adherence to national eHealth security and data privacy standards (6 points) and Domain 9: Interoperability (18 points), comprising SAQ 9-1 on identifying target health information systems (e.g. DHIS2, eLMIS, HRIS), companion applications (e.g. mobile money), and data dictionaries (9 points), and SAQ 9-2 on demonstrated adherence to government HIS data standards (e.g. HL7), clinical terminology standards (ICD-10, SNOMED CT), and other standards such as INN (9 points).

Presents self-assessment questions for Axis 4, Domain 10: Adaptability, covering SAQ 10-1 on adapting technology for new user groups and health domains with documentation and local developer modifiability (12 points), SAQ 10-2 on adapting content for new languages, illiterate users, and cultural contexts (9 points), and SAQ 10-3 on hardware and operating system transferability across mobile device types and platforms (6 points).

Provides the Axis 4: Technology & Architecture scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 8: Data (SAQs 8-1, 8-2, 8-3a, 8-3b; 45 points), Domain 9: Interoperability (SAQs 9-1, 9-2; 18 points), and Domain 10: Adaptability (SAQs 10-1, 10-2, 10-3; 27 points) to compute the overall Axis 4 percentage score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 4: Technology & Architecture, summarizing five focus areas and presenting Domain 8 (Data) guidance on integrating user feedback through user-centred design to enhance data accessibility—illustrated by JSI's iterative dashboard, resupply calculation, and alert design for the cStock supply chain system—alongside assessing development, maintenance, upgrade, and hosting costs of secondary features.

Continues Axis 4, Domain 8 (Data) planning guidance with field lessons and tips on designing offline data collection and syncing systems for low-connectivity settings (illustrated by OpenSRP in the Dristhi project in India and Medic Mobile), weighing cloud versus in-country server data hosting approaches and building government hosting capacity in line with WHO–ITU guidelines, and developing realistic projections for data transmission, warehousing, and storage capacity (illustrated by JSI's cStock expansion).

Provides Domain 8 guidance on establishing user-specific data access privileges, inactivity password prompts, staff confidentiality training, and national data protection compliance, followed by Domain 9 (Interoperability) guidance on planning for interoperability from the outset with national HIS, eLMIS, HRIS, and OpenHIE architectures and registries.

Describes using application programming interfaces (APIs) to facilitate systems interoperability—highlighted by Uganda's mTrac and DHIS2 integration using the OpenHIE Facility Registry Database API to resolve facility naming mismatches—and presents Domain 10 (Adaptability) guidance on fostering a culture of systematic documentation using wikis and code version control repositories such as GitHub.

Lists four Axis 4 resources on digital development, device selection, privacy law, and interoperability training: Principles for Digital Development, CommCare Help's Choosing a Device Type (2015), TrustLaw and mHealth Alliance's Patient Privacy in a Mobile World (2013), and the DHIS2 Academy workshop series.

Continues the Axis 4 resource directory with four standards, interoperability, and policy repositories: Open Concept Lab (OCL), mHealth Alliance's The State of Standards and Interoperability for mHealth among Low- and Middle-Income Countries (Payne, 2013), Open Health Information Exchange (OpenHIE), and WHO's Global Observatory for eHealth Directory of eHealth Policies (2015).
Section divider page introducing Axis 5: Operations within the six-axis MAPS Toolkit navigation framework.

Presents Section A (Thematic overview) for Axis 5: Operations across Domain 11 (Personnel), Domain 12 (Training and support), Domain 13 (Outreach and sensitization), and Domain 14 (Contingency planning), detailing Domain 11 requirements for workforce projection, role redefinition, retention, knowledge management, and four core leadership roles (director/advisor, manager, systems administrator, financial manager), and defining end-users and secondary users.

Continues the Axis 5 thematic overview across Domain 12 (Training and support: tailored user training, routine field supervision, and tiered local/expert technical support), Domain 13 (Outreach and sensitization: engaging implementing partner staff, government officials, and community leaders/members), and Domain 14 (Contingency planning: procedures for connectivity and power constraints and device retention against loss, theft, breakage, and misuse).

Presents Section B (Self-assessment questions) for Axis 5, Domain 11: Personnel (33 points), comprising SAQ 11-1 on projecting personnel needs, restructuring job descriptions, expanding capacity, defining roles, retaining staff, preserving institutional knowledge, and updating workload/salary policies (21 points), and SAQ 11-2 on appointing a strategic advisor/director, operational manager, systems administrator, and financial manager (12 points).

Presents self-assessment questions for Axis 5, Domain 12: Training and support (45 points), covering SAQ 12-1a on initial training, operational guides/SOPs, refresher training, secondary user training, and training resources for health-worker-focused or client-focused products (15 or 6 points), and SAQ 12-1b on user literacy alignment, training delivery mechanisms, curricula, and competency/certification quality assurance (12 points).

Continues Axis 5 self-assessment questions with SAQ 12-2 on organizational structures, resources, and problem-resolution training for ongoing end-user supervision (9 points), SAQ 12-3 on local first-line technical support teams, escalation procedures, and peer-champion user support (9 points), and Domain 13: Outreach and sensitization SAQ 13-1 on orienting implementing partners, government representatives, and community leaders (9 points).

Completes Axis 5 self-assessment questions with SAQ 13-2 on community mobilization and community feedback events (6 points) and Domain 14: Contingency planning (18 points), comprising SAQ 14-1 on procedures and SOPs for connectivity and electricity constraints such as multi-SIM use and solar chargers (9 points) and SAQ 14-2 on preventing device loss/theft, stakeholder-vetted replacement policies/contracts, and preventing device misuse (9 points).

Provides the Axis 5: Operations scorecard for tallying points and computing domain percentages across Domain 11: Personnel (33 points), Domain 12: Training and support (45 or 36 points), Domain 13: Outreach and sensitization (15 points), and Domain 14: Contingency planning (18 points) to calculate the overall Axis 5 percentage score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 5: Operations, summarizing five operational planning priorities and providing Domain 11 (Personnel) guidance on maintaining programme documentation and abbreviated training packages to mitigate staff turnover, and empowering staff across administrative levels to reduce reliance on external technical support (illustrated by JSI's multi-level cStock training in Malawi).

Provides Axis 5, Domain 12 (Training and support) guidance on dedicating time to device familiarization, dummy-server demo modes, and technology-literacy grouping, reinforcing classroom instruction with at least four weeks of on-the-job follow-up training and supportive supervision, and Table 5 comparing peer champions (Pathfinder International and D-Tree in the United Republic of Tanzania) and integration with existing health content and certificates (IRD vaccinators in Pakistan).

Continues Axis 5 planning guidance with partnering with local university computer science and informatics programmes for first-line technical support (Domain 12), and Domain 13 (Outreach and sensitization) guidance on developing standard operating procedures (SOPs) and checklists to delineate stakeholder roles and allocating continuous resources and engagement strategies for community mobilization with local and religious leaders.

Provides guidance on limiting mobile device misuse through application blockers and remote device management/tracking software (such as Meraki System Manager), and introduces Domain 14 (Contingency planning) lessons on designing around low-resource technical environments, illustrated by Medic Mobile's field assessment of coverage and power in Katanga Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, using basic handsets and solar chargers.

Details Domain 14 strategies for minimizing device loss and theft—highlighting D-Tree and Pathfinder International's group stipend pool accountability model and personal-use allowance among community health workers in Shinyanga, United Republic of Tanzania, and MOTECH Ghana's handset receipt agreement sharing replacement costs (75% negligent nurse, 25% facility staff)—and compares the pros and cons of project-sponsored device procurement versus using end-users' personal phones.

Lists three Axis 5 operational and training resources: Grameen Foundation's Mobile Technology for Community Health in Ghana: What it Is and What Grameen Foundation has Learned So Far (2012), mPowering Frontline Health Workers' ORB open-licensed training library, and Dimagi's CommCare Help: Mobile User Survey Templates (2012).
Section divider page introducing Axis 6: Monitoring & Evaluation within the six-axis MAPS Toolkit navigation framework.

Presents Section A (Thematic overview) for Axis 6: Monitoring & Evaluation across Domain 15 (Process monitoring: 15-1 programme fidelity, 15-2 optimization) and Domain 16 (Evaluation research: 16-1 evaluation systems, 16-2 evidence claims, 16-3 dissemination), detailing Domain 15 requirements for budgeting (e.g. DFID's recommended 10% M&E allocation), Performance Monitoring Plans (PMPs), dashboards/scorecards, user feedback, and course correction, and defining process monitoring, evaluation research, and programme fidelity.

Presents the thematic overview for Axis 6, Domain 16 (Evaluation research), covering funding and external evaluators, aligning with stakeholder evidence priorities, developing a theory of change or logical framework linking inputs to impacts, combining system-generated and human-collected data, securing ethical approval, articulating outcomes across three levels (health systems, provider/service delivery, and individual health status) plus cost-effectiveness, defining indicators and comparators, and disseminating findings locally and widely.

Presents Section B (Self-assessment questions) for Axis 6, Domain 15: Process monitoring (25 points), comprising SAQ 15-1a on earmarking monitoring funds and internal staff (4 points), SAQ 15-1b on developing a Performance Monitoring Plan (PMP), indicators/sources, and measurement instruments (9 points), and SAQ 15-2 on regular data analysis processes, implementation dashboards/scorecards, user feedback mechanisms, and course-correction protocols (12 points).

Presents self-assessment questions for Axis 6, Domain 16: Evaluation research (66 points), covering SAQ 16-1a on evaluation funding, internal staff, and external evaluators (6 points), SAQ 16-1b on articulating stakeholder evidence priorities, developing a theory of change/logical framework, and obtaining ethical approval (9 points), SAQ 16-1c on accessing system-generated and human-collected data streams (6 points), and SAQ 16-2a on articulating health systems, provider/service delivery, client, and population health outcomes (12 points).

Completes Axis 6, Domain 16 self-assessment questions with SAQ 16-2b on defining outcome indicators, data sources, quantitative/qualitative methods, and collection frequency/comparators (12 points), SAQ 16-2c on carrying out data collection to support evidence claims across technology functionality, usability, efficacy, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness/cost-utility (15 points), and SAQ 16-3 on identifying local and wider dissemination opportunities (6 points).

Provides the Axis 6: Monitoring & Evaluation scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 15: Process monitoring (SAQs 15-1a, 15-1b, 15-2; 25 points) and Domain 16: Evaluation research (SAQs 16-1a through 16-3; 66 or 60 points) to compute the overall Axis 6 percentage score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 6: Monitoring & Evaluation, outlining five key planning functions and presenting Domain 15 (Process monitoring) guidance on planning early for capturing, formatting, documenting, and structuring system-generated operational data (such as timestamps, GPS coordinates, and worker IDs) across back-end servers and MNO partnerships.

Continues Axis 6, Domain 15 planning guidance with field lessons on using process monitoring data for continuous service delivery improvement (VillageReach's Chipatala cha pa Foni hotline in Malawi adjusting message timing and staff allocation), enforcing data quality and integrity against fabricated reporting in pay-for-performance schemes (D-Tree International's timestamp, GPS, and suspicious activity monitoring in the United Republic of Tanzania), and using CommCare Help's Worker Activity and Form Completion Time reports to inform a Performance Monitoring Plan (PMP).

Provides Axis 6, Domain 16 (Evaluation research) guidance on anticipating ethical review complexities for mHealth data security/privacy, multi-institutional approvals, and telephone informed consent scripts, and illustrates organizing comprehensive M&E systems using the Virginia Tech RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework as applied by KEMRI's Texting to Improve Testing (TextIT) early infant HIV testing trial in Kenya.

Illustrates using logical frameworks to link mHealth inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts—featuring an adapted MNCH logical framework for South Africa's MomConnect programme aiming to reduce maternal, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality—and advises aligning evaluation indicators with national health strategies and stakeholder evidence priorities, as demonstrated by KEMRI's TextIT study.

Describes harnessing mobile phones for evaluation data collection alongside service delivery—illustrated by FHI 360's SMS user surveys for m4RH in the United Republic of Tanzania while accounting for selection bias and survey fatigue—and introduces two evaluation resources: Mobile Alliance for Maternal Action's MAMA's Research Agenda (2015) and the World Bank's Impact Evaluation in Practice (Gertler et al., 2011).

Concludes the Axis 6 resource listing with Knowledge4Health's mHealthEvidence.org literature repository and the WHO mHealth Technical Evidence Review Group's Guidelines for Reporting mHealth Evidence: the mHealth Evidence Reporting and Assessment (mERA) checklist (Agarwal et al.).

Provides the master Summary Scorecard for recording and comparing overall axis and domain percentage scores across all six MAPS Toolkit axes (Groundwork, Partnerships, Financial Health, Technology & Architecture, Operations, and Monitoring & Evaluation) and their 16 domains.

Lists bibliographic references 1 through 15 cited in The MAPS Toolkit, including K4Health, PMNCH, Institute of Medicine, World Health Assembly Resolution WHA58.28 on eHealth, ExpandNet/WHO scaling-up guides, Labrique et al. (2013), HIMSS interoperability definitions, USAID's Idea to Impact, LiST modelling studies, and the Columbia University mHealth barriers policy white paper.

Concludes the bibliography with references 16 through 27, covering the Bellagio eHealth Evaluation Call to Action, the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit (2012), complex adaptive systems and African mHealth systematic reviews, WHO mTERG working papers, Mehl & Labrique (2014), Advanced Development for Africa partnership reports, Vital Wave Consulting sustainable financing reports, AIDSTAR-Two, and the World Bank Group M&E handbook.

Presents Annex 1, detailing the multi-year methodology used to develop the MAPS Toolkit (2011–2015), including Innovation Working Group (IWG) grantee workshops, literature and project report reviews, qualitative site visits (May 2014), expert consultations (June–October 2014), self-assessment question (SAQ) review panels (January–March 2015), a multi-agency technical workshop (April 2015), pre-testing in Malawi (May 2015), and six global and in-country learning workshops.

Begins Annex 2 (Projects that informed 'Lessons from the field'), profiling five IWG grantee and affiliate mHealth deployments: Dimagi's CommCare for ASHAs in India, D-Tree International's eNUT child malnutrition guideline software in Zanzibar (United Republic of Tanzania), FHI 360's m4RH contraceptive SMS service in Kenya and the United Republic of Tanzania, Grameen Foundation's MOTECH (Mobile Midwife and Nurses Application) in Ghana and Nigeria, and Georgetown University IRH's CycleTel family planning SMS service in India.

Continues Annex 2 with profiles of seven mHealth projects: Interactive Research and Development's (IRD) Interactive Alerts immunization lottery and RFID tracker in Pakistan, IICD's MAMMA malaria surveillance application in Mali and Senegal, John Snow, Inc.'s (JSI) cStock community supply chain system in Malawi, KEMRI's TextIT PMTCT retention trial in Kenya, Medic Mobile's SafeSim maternal and neonatal platform in Nepal, Rwanda MOH and UNICEF's RapidSMS maternal and newborn tracking system, and Zanzibar MOH's Wired Mothers (mama mitandao) antenatal/postnatal SMS service.

Concludes Annex 2 with profiles of four mHealth initiatives: Pathfinder International's CommCare decision-support scale-up under Nigeria's Saving One Million Lives initiative, the Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty's (SERP) mNDCC nutrition monitoring application in Andhra Pradesh, India, UNICEF and the Ugandan MOH's mTrac HMIS reporting and U-Report citizen feedback system in Uganda, and VillageReach's Chipatala cha pa Foni maternal and child health hotline in Malawi.
